lessons.title: What you are actually talking to

exercises.prompt: You type a question. Before writing anything, what does the model work out first?
exercises.feedback: It does not plan an answer and then write it down. It works out one word, commits to it, then works out the next one with that word now part of the input. Everything else in this course follows from that single loop.

exercises.prompt: The model has written "The capital of France is". What are the chances the next word is Paris?

config.question: How likely is Paris?
config.reveal: Almost certain, because in nearly every sentence the model ever saw with that opening, Paris followed. Now try "My favourite city is". The model has no basis to prefer any city, so the probability spreads thin across hundreds of them. Same machine, completely different confidence, and the only thing that changed was how much the sentence constrained what could come next.

exercises.feedback: Your prompt is doing exactly this to every word of the answer. A vague prompt leaves the field wide open, and wide open means average.

exercises.prompt: Which of these openings leave the model with an obvious continuation?
exercises.feedback: The three wide-open ones are the shape of most first drafts of a prompt. They are not wrong, exactly. They just hand the model a decision you could have made yourself, and it will make it blandly, because blandness is what the average of everything looks like.

exercises.prompt: Why does one badly chosen opening word sometimes derail a whole answer?

options.text: Later words are chosen given earlier ones
The model cannot edit what it has written
An error early on lowers its confidence

exercises.feedback: B is true and is not the reason. The model does not need to edit, because it never intended anything different. Each word narrows what can sensibly follow, so a wrong turn early makes every later word a sensible continuation of the wrong thing.

exercises.prompt: Three of these describe what the model is doing. Which does NOT?

options.text: Continuing text one piece at a time
Using the words so far as its input
Consulting a stored table of facts

exercises.feedback: There is no table inside. That is why it handles a question nobody has ever asked, and also why it can be fluently wrong about a date.

exercises.prompt: Match what you noticed to what is behind it.

pairs.right: Those patterns are dense in training
Thin patterns, weaker constraint

pairs.left: It never says it has not seen this
pairs.right: Every input still yields a next word

pairs.left: It writes fluently even when wrong
pairs.right: Fluency and truth are separate

exercises.feedback: Four observations that all trace back to the same loop.

exercises.prompt: You want help preparing for a job interview. Which prompt gets you further?

config.b: I have a first-round interview for a junior data analyst role at a logistics company on Friday. Give me six questions they are likely to ask and what a strong answer covers.

exercises.feedback: B is not better because it is longer. It is better because almost every word removes a possibility. Role, seniority, industry, timing, and the shape of the output you want are five constraints the model no longer has to guess.

exercises.prompt: What is the most useful thing a longer prompt usually adds?
exercises.feedback: Length in itself does nothing. A rambling paragraph that never says who the answer is for constrains nothing. Ask what each sentence rules out, and if the answer is nothing, cut it.

lessons.title: The four parts of a prompt

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a prompt to its job.

pairs.right: Says what to do
Supplies the background
The thing to work on
Sets the shape of the answer

exercises.feedback: Four jobs, and you rarely need all four. Naming them matters because when an answer disappoints, the fix is usually a missing one rather than a rewrite.

exercises.prompt: Sort each fragment by which part of the prompt it is.

items.text: I am writing for first-year students

exercises.feedback: Most prompts that disappoint are missing one of these four rather than being badly worded.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part that leaves too much undecided.

config.text: Rewrite this to be more professional. Here is the text: hey can u send the file when free thanks

exercises.feedback: Professional for whom? A message to a close colleague and a message to someone you have never met are both professional and look nothing alike. This is a context gap, and the model will fill it with the blandest reading available.

exercises.prompt: Add the output indicator.

config.template: Summarise the report below for someone who has ten seconds. ___

exercises.feedback: The other three sound like instructions and constrain nothing. Be thorough does not tell the model whether thorough means two lines or two pages.

exercises.prompt: Assemble a working prompt.

tiles: You are helping a nurse on a night shift
flag anything needing a doctor tonight

exercises.feedback: Order is flexible, presence is not. Drop the context and it writes for nobody in particular. Drop the bullet count and you get three paragraphs at 3am.

exercises.prompt: Three of these are output indicators. Which is NOT?

options.text: Reply as a table with two columns
Keep it under a hundred words

exercises.feedback: The style guide is context. It is material the model should draw on, not a description of the shape of the answer. Context feeds the answer, output indicators constrain it.

exercises.prompt: An answer is accurate but written at the wrong level for your reader. Which part of the prompt was weak?

options.text: Context, since the reader is unnamed
Instruction, since the task was vague
Input data, since too little was given

exercises.feedback: The model did the task correctly. It just had no idea who it was for, so it picked a default reader, and the default reader is nobody in particular.

exercises.prompt: Both prompts contain the same information. Which will behave more predictably?

config.a: Explain compound interest simply and briefly for a 14-year-old who is confused about it and use an example.
config.b: Explain compound interest. Reader: a confused 14-year-old. Include one worked example. Under 120 words.

exercises.feedback: Same content, sorted into its four jobs. B is easier for you to edit later too, because when the answer is wrong you can see which line to change.

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase that constrains the least.

config.text: Write a short, engaging, professional post about our new product launch that really connects with our audience.

exercises.feedback: Every prompt has one of these. It feels like the most important sentence and it is the only one carrying no information. Which audience, connecting over what, and how would you know if it had worked?

exercises.prompt: Does each phrase actually narrow the answer?

items.text: For readers who have never invested

exercises.feedback: The second bucket is where most prompt-writing effort goes and where none of the value is. A useful test: could two people disagree about whether the answer met it?

exercises.prompt: Which addition would most improve "Summarise this article"?

options.text: Naming who the summary is for

exercises.feedback: A summary for a specialist and a summary for a newcomer keep different things and cut different things. Without a reader there is no basis for deciding what matters, so it keeps a bit of everything.

exercises.prompt: Match each vague request to the constraint that fixes it.

pairs.right: Under 80 words
Suitable for someone you have not met
Give exactly four, each one line
For someone with no technical background

exercises.feedback: Each fix replaces a feeling with something two people could agree on.

exercises.prompt: Turn the vague instruction into a checkable one.

config.template: Rewrite this paragraph so it is easier to read. ___

exercises.feedback: The other three restate the request in different words. Only one of them could be checked by someone who was not in the room.

exercises.prompt: Three of these tell the model what NOT to do. Which does NOT?
exercises.feedback: D points at what to include, which is useful and is a different tool. Negative constraints are the most forgotten half of a prompt, and often the half that fixes an answer that keeps drifting somewhere you do not want it.

exercises.prompt: You want a reading list. Which prompt will you be happier with?

config.a: Recommend some good books on negotiation.
config.b: Recommend four books on negotiation for someone who already read Never Split the Difference. One line each on what it adds beyond that.

exercises.feedback: A gets you the four books everyone names. B rules those out by stating what you have read, which is the single most useful thing you can tell it. Constraints are not restrictions here, they are the whole mechanism.

exercises.prompt: Why does naming your reader change the answer so much?

options.text: It rules out most possible answers
The model adjusts its effort level
It makes the request feel important

exercises.feedback: Back to lesson 1. Every constraint you add narrows what can plausibly come next, and narrow is where the useful answers live.

exercises.prompt: What is the single operation everything else in this unit rests on?

options.text: Predicting the next piece of text

exercises.feedback: One loop, repeated. Hold onto it.

exercises.prompt: Sort each line by its job in the prompt.

items.text: Draft a reply to the message below
The customer has already complained twice
Two short paragraphs, no apology in the first

exercises.prompt: Your prompt gave a disappointing answer. Order the fixes to try.

steps: Say who the answer is for
Say what shape the answer should take
Add what to leave out
Supply the source material it needs

exercises.feedback: Roughly cheapest and highest-yield first. Most disappointing answers are fixed at step 1, and people usually start at step 4.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part that adds the least.

config.text: You are a world-class expert marketer with 20 years of experience. Write me an amazing product description that will drive conversions.

exercises.feedback: Naming a role can genuinely help, because it points at the kind of writing you want. Attaching a number of years to it points at nothing. There is no dial inside labelled experience.

exercises.prompt: Match each symptom to the part of the prompt that was missing.

pairs.right: Output indicator
Context
Instruction
Input data

exercises.prompt: Three of these reliably improve an answer. Which does NOT?
exercises.feedback: Effort is not a setting. Everything else on that list removes a decision the model would otherwise make for you.

exercises.prompt: You have a dense two-page policy document and a colleague who needs to act on it before a meeting in ten minutes. Write a prompt that gets them what they need.

config.goal: Produce an actionable brief from a dense document under time pressure.
config.assessed: Does the prompt name the reader, state the output shape, and say what to leave out?

exercises.prompt: Take this weak prompt and rewrite it so two different people would agree on whether the answer was any good: "Write something engaging about our company culture."

config.goal: Convert an unfalsifiable prompt into a checkable one.
config.assessed: Does the rewrite replace unfalsifiable praise words with checkable constraints, and supply a reader and a shape?

exercises.prompt: Ask a model how many R letters are in "strawberry". What does it usually say?

config.question: What does it answer?
config.reveal: Three is the right answer and the model often says two. Now type the same word spaced out, s t r a w b e r r y, and it counts correctly almost every time.

exercises.feedback: Nothing about the model reasoning changed between those two attempts. What changed was what arrived. Strawberry comes in as roughly two chunks, straw and berry, with the letters sealed inside. Spaced out, each letter arrives as its own piece, and suddenly there is something to count.

exercises.prompt: Guess how many tokens each of these becomes, then see the real count from the encoder.

config.question: Token counts
config.reveal: Counts come from the real gpt-4o-mini encoding at runtime.

exercises.feedback: Common English words usually cost one token each. Long rare words get chopped into several. Hindi costs the most pieces of all, because there was far less Devanagari in training, so the encoder never learned big reusable chunks for it.

exercises.prompt: Your Hinglish prompts use more tokens than the same message in English. Which is NOT a real consequence?

options.text: You reach the length limit sooner
The same request costs more to run
It understands the Hindi less well
Long Hindi documents fill the window

exercises.feedback: Token count is about space and money. It is not a measure of comprehension. The model can handle Hindi meaning perfectly well while paying more to hold the same number of words.

exercises.prompt: Which tasks fight against the way text is chopped up?

items.text: Reversing the spelling of a name

exercises.feedback: Everything in the first bucket needs the letters. Everything in the second works at the level of meaning, which is the level the pieces were built for. When a model fails at something that looks trivially easy, this is usually why.

exercises.prompt: Match each observation to its cause.

pairs.right: Letters are sealed inside chunks
Fewer learned chunks for Devanagari
No single chunk was learned for them
One chunk each, seen constantly

exercises.prompt: Three of these are true of tokens. Which is NOT?

options.text: A token is often part of a word
Common words are usually one token
One token always equals one word
Punctuation can be its own token

exercises.prompt: A model advertises a 128,000-token limit. Roughly how many English words is that?
exercises.feedback: Fewer words than tokens, because an average English word costs a little over one token, and more if it is unusual. The number on the box is never the number of words you get, and the gap widens for Hindi and for technical text.

exercises.prompt: A developer says a 128k limit means pasting a 128,000-word document. What is wrong?

options.text: Limits apply only to the reply

exercises.feedback: Worth adding: the limit covers everything at once. Your instructions, the pasted document, and the answer it writes all come out of the same budget.

exercises.prompt: What is the context window?

options.text: The text it can consider at once
The memory it keeps between chats
The time before a session expires

exercises.feedback: B is the more useful misconception to clear up. By default nothing carries between conversations. Anything that looks like memory is a system pasting earlier text back in for you.

exercises.prompt: In a single long chat, what counts against the window?

items.text: Everything it has replied so far
A document you pasted at the start
A file on your laptop you mentioned
A link you pasted without contents

exercises.feedback: The last two are the ones that catch people. Naming a document is not the same as supplying it. A link without a tool to fetch it is just some characters that look like a URL.

exercises.prompt: You have a 400-token budget and more material than fits. Pack the desk for the question: what did we agree about delivery dates?

tiles: The signed contract clause on delivery (120)

exercises.feedback: The full contract does not fit and would not help more than the clause that answers the question. Packing well is not about fitting the most in. It is about leaving out everything that does not bear on what you asked.

exercises.prompt: A 200-page document will not fit. Order a workable approach.

steps: Split it into sections
Summarise each section on its own
Combine the summaries
Ask your question of the combined summary

exercises.feedback: Something is lost at every join, which is the honest trade. A claim that depends on page 12 and page 190 together can disappear in the middle of this, so it is worth asking your question of a targeted section too.

exercises.prompt: Tap the assumption that will fail.

config.text: As we discussed in our conversation yesterday, please continue drafting the section on refunds.
config.span: As we discussed in our conversation yesterday

exercises.feedback: Yesterday conversation is not there. The model will not say so either. It will infer something plausible about refunds from the words in front of it and carry on confidently, which is worse than an error message.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to what is happening.

pairs.left: It forgets an instruction from earlier
pairs.right: Long chat, early text crowded out

pairs.left: It contradicts a fact you gave
pairs.right: Detail buried mid-prompt

pairs.left: It cannot see a file you named
pairs.right: Never supplied, only mentioned

pairs.left: It repeats itself in long replies
pairs.right: Its own output is filling the window

exercises.prompt: You paste 60 pages and ask about one clause. Where is it riskiest for that clause to sit?
exercises.feedback: Beginnings and endings get attended to more reliably than the middle. Fitting inside the window is necessary and not sufficient, which is the argument for pulling out the ten relevant pages rather than pasting all sixty.

exercises.prompt: Three of these help with a document that is too long. Which does NOT?

options.text: Ask it to read more carefully
Ask about one section at a time

exercises.prompt: Which prompt produces a summary you can use?

config.b: Summarise this report for someone deciding whether to fund the project. Five bullets, each naming a number or a date.

exercises.feedback: A summary with no reader keeps a little of everything, because it has no basis for deciding what matters. Naming the decision the reader has to make is the single most useful sentence you can add.

exercises.prompt: Which of these actually shape a summary?

items.text: For a reader with no background
Keep every figure, drop the narrative

exercises.feedback: Comprehensive yet concise asks for both ends of the only real dial in summarising. It reads like direction and lands as noise.

exercises.prompt: Add the line that guards against a quietly dropped detail.

config.template: Summarise the document below in six bullets. ___
bank: Quote the line each bullet came from.
config.correct: Quote the line each bullet came from.

exercises.feedback: The other three are requests for diligence, which is not a thing you can request. Asking for the source line makes an omission visible, because a bullet with no line behind it stands out.

exercises.prompt: Tap the instruction that cancels itself out.

config.text: Give me a detailed yet brief summary of the attached research covering all the key points and insights.

exercises.prompt: Your summary of a long document missed a critical clause. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The clause sat deep in the middle
The model does not read clauses

exercises.prompt: Match each problem with a summary to its fix.

pairs.right: Name the decision the reader faces
Ask for figures to be preserved
Ask for a source line per point
State a bullet count or word limit

exercises.prompt: Order a reliable way to summarise a long report you have never read.

steps: Ask for a one-line description of what the document is
Ask for the section headings
Summarise the sections that bear on your question
Ask for anything important that those sections left out

exercises.feedback: Step 4 is the one people skip. You are asking about material you have not read, so your question may have pointed at the wrong sections, and this is the cheapest way to find that out.

exercises.prompt: What most improves a summary of a very long document?

options.text: Asking it to be more thorough

exercises.feedback: This is the whole unit in one line. Capacity is not the binding constraint. Relevance is.

exercises.prompt: Why is spelling a persistent weakness and summarising a persistent strength?
Which of these will the model be able to use?

items.text: Text you pasted into this chat
A section you summarised earlier in this chat
A file sitting on your desktop
Something you told it in a chat last week
A link with no page contents attached

exercises.prompt: You paste a 40-page report and then hold a long back-and-forth about it. What runs out first?
exercises.feedback: The conversation grows and the document does not. In a long session your own earlier exchanges are usually the first thing pushed out, which is why an instruction you gave twenty messages ago quietly stops being followed.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part that will not survive contact with reality.

config.text: Read the whole 300-page manual carefully and give me a complete summary that does not miss anything important.

exercises.feedback: Three hundred pages likely exceeds what fits, and even where it fits the middle is attended to least. Worse, there is no way to tell from the output what was dropped. A prompt that cannot fail visibly is a prompt you cannot trust.

exercises.prompt: Match each symptom to its underlying cause.

pairs.right: Tokens hide the letters
Context window filled up
Attention weakest in the middle
Fewer learned chunks

exercises.prompt: Three of these reduce the risk of a dropped detail. Which does NOT?

options.text: Ask for a source line per point
Work one section at a time
Tell it not to miss anything

exercises.prompt: You have a 50-page rental agreement and two hours to decide whether to sign. Write a prompt that gets you a decision-ready summary you could be held to.

config.goal: Produce a defensible sign/do-not-sign summary from a long document.
config.assessed: Does the prompt name the decision, constrain the output shape, ask for evidence lines, and handle material that will not fit?

exercises.prompt: A summary you received is fluent and useless: correct in every sentence, but it never says what the reader should do. Write a prompt that would have produced a better one.

config.goal: Turn a decorative summary into an actionable one.
config.assessed: Does the rewrite supply a reader and a decision, and replace unfalsifiable words with checkable constraints?

lessons.title: It does not know it is wrong

exercises.prompt: A lawyer asks an AI for cases supporting an argument. It returns a case name, a citation number and a date. None of it exists. What happened?

options.text: It produced text shaped like a real citation
It copied a case from another country's courts
It searched the web and trusted a bad source

exercises.feedback: The model was never looking anything up. It generates the shape of a citation, because citations in its training data have a shape, and a fabricated one fits that shape just as neatly as a real one. This is why invented sources look so convincing: plausibility is the only thing being optimised.

exercises.prompt: Which of these can a model answer from what it learned during training?

items.text: The plot of a novel published in 1998

exercises.feedback: Two different walls here, and it is worth keeping them apart. Training data stops at a date, so recent events are missing. Private information was never in there at all. A model can be given either one, but it has to be handed over in the conversation.

exercises.prompt: A model describes a 2019 event in detail but knows nothing about last week. Why?

options.text: Its training data stops at a fixed date
Recent events sit behind a paid tier

exercises.feedback: Training happens once, over a fixed body of text, and then stops. Nothing decays afterwards. C gets the direction backwards: older material is the part it knows best.

exercises.prompt: Match each failure to what caused it.

pairs.left: Invented a book title that does not exist
pairs.right: Generated a plausible shape, not a fact

pairs.left: Named a CEO who left three years ago
pairs.right: Training data has a cutoff date

pairs.left: Could not tell you your order status
pairs.right: No access to your private systems

pairs.left: Gave a different answer each time you asked
pairs.right: Word choice involves randomness

exercises.feedback: Four failures that feel identical from the outside and need four different fixes. Telling them apart is most of the skill.

exercises.prompt: Three of these are hallucinations. Which is NOT?

options.text: Inventing a research paper that was never written
Giving the wrong year for a real historical event
Declining to answer because the topic is sensitive
Making up a quote and attributing it to a real person

exercises.feedback: A refusal is the model choosing not to answer. That might frustrate you, but nothing false has been produced. The distinction matters because the fixes point in opposite directions: refusals need rephrasing, fabrications need a source.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part of this prompt that will not work reliably.

config.text: Tell me about the safety record of the Tata Nexon and cite your sources.

exercises.feedback: Asking for citations from memory is an invitation to invent them. The model will produce something citation-shaped because you asked for something citation-shaped. Citations only mean anything when they point at documents you supplied or that a search tool actually fetched.

exercises.prompt: Both prompts ask the same question. Which one can you trust more?

config.a: What are the main provisions of India's DPDP Act?
config.b: Here is the text of India's DPDP Act. What are its main provisions?

options.text: The answer is tied to text you supplied
Naming the source improves its recall

exercises.feedback: B changes the job from remembering to reading. Only one of those is something the model is reliably good at.

exercises.prompt: You need a fact you can actually rely on. What is the strongest move?

options.text: Paste the document and ask about it
Ask the model to double-check itself
Ask the same question three times

exercises.feedback: B and C both ask a confident guesser to audit its own guess, and it will confidently agree with itself. A changes what the model is doing.

exercises.prompt: This is an AI-written paragraph. Tap the detail you would check first.

config.text: The Assam tea industry began with Robert Bruce's expedition in 1823. His findings were published in The Botanical Survey of Upper Assam (1826), which remains the standard reference on the subject.
config.span: The Botanical Survey of Upper Assam (1826)

exercises.feedback: Named title, with a year in brackets. That is exactly the format a fabrication takes, because the format is what the model is imitating. A specific titled source with a specific year is the highest-risk element in the paragraph, and it is checkable in seconds.

exercises.prompt: Why does a fabricated answer often feel more trustworthy than a hedged one?

options.text: Hedging means the model is guessing

exercises.feedback: Nothing in the writing quality tracks truth. A model producing a fabrication is doing the same thing it does when it is right, and it is equally good at it. Fluency is not a signal, which is uncomfortable, because fluency is the signal most of us use with people.

exercises.prompt: Which claims would you verify before using them?

items.text: A quoted sentence with a source
A general explanation of how interest works
A summary of a document you supplied
The definition of a common term

exercises.feedback: The pattern is worth naming: the more specific and checkable a claim is, the more likely it was generated rather than known. General explanations are safe because they are the pattern the model genuinely learned. Precise identifiers are where invention hides.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim to the fastest way to check it.

pairs.right: Search a library catalogue
Go to the official statistics body

pairs.left: A quote from a public figure
pairs.right: Find the original speech or interview

pairs.left: A summary of your own document
pairs.right: Reread the relevant section

exercises.feedback: Verification is usually cheaper than it feels. The reason people skip it is that fluent prose does not trigger the instinct to check.

exercises.prompt: Complete the prompt so the model cannot invent anything.

config.template: Using only the text below, answer the question. If the answer is not in the text, say ___.

exercises.feedback: Without that final clause, a model asked a question the document does not answer will fill the gap rather than leave it. Giving it an explicit permitted exit is what stops that.

exercises.prompt: Three of these make fabrication more likely. Which does NOT?

options.text: Asking about a very obscure local topic
Asking for exact figures from memory
Pasting the source document in chat
Asking for sources without giving any

exercises.feedback: The other three all ask the model to produce specifics it has no access to. Obscure topics are thin in training data, so the pattern it falls back on is weaker and the invention more confident.

exercises.prompt: An AI gives you a statistic. You ask "are you sure?" and it apologises and changes the number. What does that tell you?

options.text: It caught its own earlier mistake

exercises.feedback: Pushing back changes what text is likely to come next, and an apology is extremely likely text after a challenge. The model did not go and check. It has no way to. Treat a retraction as evidence about the conversation, not about the number.

exercises.prompt: You want reliable background on a new regulation. Which prompt?

config.a: Summarise the new regulation and list the penalties.
config.b: From the attached PDF, list each penalty and quote the line it comes from.

exercises.feedback: B does two things at once: it points at a source, and it asks for the quote, which makes checking cheap. A prompt that makes verification easy is worth more than one that makes the answer sound polished.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps in order for a system that answers questions from your own documents.

steps: Break the documents into chunks
Find the chunks closest to the question
Put those chunks into the prompt
Ask the model to answer using only those chunks

exercises.feedback: This is retrieval-augmented generation, and the ordering is the whole idea: search first, generate second. The model never searches. Something else does the finding, then hands over what it found.

exercises.prompt: What does grounding an answer actually mean?

options.text: The answer comes from supplied text
The model is set to a lower temperature
The model has been trained on your data

exercises.feedback: C is the common and expensive misunderstanding. You almost never need to train anything. You need to put the right text in front of the model at the moment you ask.

exercises.prompt: Build a research prompt you can trust. Drag the tiles into place.

tiles: quote the sentence each one appears in
if a date is missing, write "not stated"

exercises.feedback: Four separate jobs, and dropping any one of them opens a different hole. Without the source constraint it draws on memory. Without the quote requirement you cannot check it. Without the gap instruction it fills silence with plausible dates.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to what it does.

pairs.right: Ties the answer to text you provide
Finds the right text to provide
Points at where a claim came from
Marks where training data stopped

exercises.feedback: Four words that get used interchangeably in marketing copy and mean four different things in practice.

exercises.prompt: You want to ground an answer in a 40-page report. Roughly how much of it fits in a model with a 128,000-token window?
exercises.feedback: Reports are smaller than they feel. The constraint you hit in practice is rarely raw capacity. It is that a model attends less reliably to material buried in the middle of a very long prompt, which is an argument for retrieving the relevant ten pages rather than pasting all forty.

exercises.prompt: Fix a model that keeps inventing details about your product. Which of these would help?

items.text: Paste the product documentation into the prompt
Tell it to answer only from that documentation
Give it a way to say the answer is not there
Tell it to be accurate and not make things up
Ask it to rate its own confidence

exercises.feedback: The three that do not help all ask the model to police itself, and self-policing is exactly the thing it cannot do. Instructions about honesty do not give it access to facts it never had.

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase doing the least work.

config.text: You are an expert analyst with deep knowledge of Indian tax law. Be accurate and never invent anything. What are the current GST slabs?

exercises.feedback: It reads like a safeguard and functions as decoration. The model is not withholding accuracy pending instructions. If current slabs are past its cutoff, that sentence changes nothing about whether it invents them. Compare with pasting the current notification and asking it to read.

exercises.prompt: Your grounded system returns a confident answer that is wrong, and the correct information was in your documents. Where is the fault most likely?

options.text: The temperature is set too high

exercises.feedback: If the right passage never made it into the prompt, the model was answering a question it had no material for. Most failures blamed on the model are failures in what got selected and handed to it.

exercises.prompt: What single fact best explains why fabricated citations look so real?

options.text: Real citations have a learnable shape
Fake sources exist in the training data
The model prefers not to admit gaps

exercises.feedback: The model learned what a citation looks like, not which ones exist. Producing a convincing fake costs it exactly as much effort as producing a real one.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the best response.

pairs.right: Supply the report

pairs.left: Need a definition of a common term
pairs.right: Just ask

pairs.left: Need a quote from a specific book
pairs.right: Supply the book, ask for the line

pairs.left: Need something from your internal wiki
pairs.right: Retrieve the page first

exercises.feedback: The question to ask before every prompt: could this have been in the training data, and would I know if it was wrong?

exercises.prompt: You have an AI-written brief to check before sending. Order the steps.

steps: Mark every specific claim: names, numbers, dates, titles
Check the marked claims against a real source
Rewrite or delete anything that fails
Send

exercises.feedback: Deliberately dull, and that is the point. Verification is not a judgement call about which parts feel wrong. Fluency gives you no signal, so you check the checkable things regardless of how confident the prose sounds.

exercises.prompt: Which of these need you to supply information?

items.text: A change in law made last month
The structure of a business letter

exercises.feedback: Recent, private, or specific to you means supply it. Stable and general means just ask.

exercises.prompt: Tap what makes this request unreliable.

config.text: Research the top five EV manufacturers in India, with market share figures and a source for each.
config.span: market share figures and a source for each

exercises.feedback: Precise numbers plus sources, requested from memory, on a topic that changes every few months. Every element of that request points at invention. Fix it by giving it a current report, or by using a tool that actually searches.

exercises.prompt: Three of these are ways to make an answer checkable. Which is NOT?

options.text: Ask it to quote the line it used
Ask it how confident it feels
Require it to flag missing information

exercises.feedback: A confidence score from a model is generated text like everything else. It reads like a measurement and it is not one.

exercises.prompt: Someone forwards you a 30-page contract and asks what you are committing to. Write a prompt that gets a reliable answer you could defend in a meeting.

config.goal: Get a defensible summary of what you are agreeing to from a supplied contract.
config.assessed: Does the prompt constrain the model to the supplied text, ask for quoted evidence, and give an explicit instruction for information that is not present?

exercises.prompt: A colleague sends you an AI-written market summary full of specific figures and no sources. Write a prompt that turns it into something you can verify, without pretending the numbers are already trustworthy.

config.goal: Convert an unsourced AI summary into a verifiable checklist.
config.assessed: Does the prompt separate checkable claims from general statements, and avoid asking the model to confirm its own earlier output?

lessons.title: Meaning depends on the sentence around it

exercises.prompt: In "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big", what does the model have to work out?
exercises.feedback: No amount of word matching gets you there. Deciding that it means the trophy needs the relationship between fitting, size and container. This is what attention does, and it is why translation between languages with different grammar works at all.

exercises.prompt: Which of these sentences cannot be translated correctly without more context?
exercises.feedback: The ambiguous three are ambiguous in English and force a choice in most other languages, where cool splits into temperature and approval, and formality has to be picked before you can write the verb.

exercises.prompt: Tap what is missing.

config.text: Translate this into Hindi: Let me know if you need anything.
config.span: Let me know if you need anything.

exercises.feedback: Hindi requires you to choose a level of formality before you can write the verb. Speaking to a teacher, a friend and a younger cousin gives three different sentences. Without being told, the model picks one and hands it over with no indication that a choice was made.

exercises.prompt: Match each reader to the register to ask for.

pairs.right: Formal, standard vocabulary
Casual, contractions fine

pairs.left: A customer you have not met
pairs.right: Polite, plain, no slang
Direct, technical terms kept

exercises.prompt: You are translating a refund policy for customers. Which prompt?

config.b: Translate this policy into Tamil for customers reading it on a phone. Keep it formal, and leave product names in English.

exercises.feedback: Formality, reading context and a rule about what not to translate. The third one matters more than it looks, because product names are exactly what a model will helpfully translate into something nobody searches for.

exercises.prompt: Three of these change how a translation should read. Which does NOT?
Add the line that resolves the ambiguity before it happens.

config.template: Translate the following support replies into Hindi. ___

exercises.feedback: The other three describe translation itself rather than making any decision. Only one of them removes a choice the model would otherwise make silently and inconsistently across a hundred replies.

exercises.prompt: Why can the same English sentence produce different translations on different runs?

lessons.title: It does not know every language equally

exercises.prompt: Why does the same sentence cost more tokens in Hindi than in English?
exercises.feedback: It is about how much of that script the encoder saw while being built, not about the language itself. A script that appeared less often gets chopped into smaller pieces, and smaller pieces means more of them.

exercises.prompt: You are budgeting for an app that answers in Hindi. Compared with the same content in English, plan for roughly how many tokens?
exercises.feedback: Worth building into your costs rather than discovering later. The same conversation in a less-represented script fills the context window sooner and costs more per exchange, for content of identical length.

exercises.prompt: Where should you be most careful trusting a translation?

items.text: A regional language with little written material online
Legal terms with no direct equivalent

exercises.feedback: The pattern is the same one from Unit 3. Thin training data means a weaker pattern to fall back on, and the output stays just as fluent while getting less reliable. Fluency will not warn you.

exercises.prompt: A model translates into a language with very little online presence. What is the risk?

options.text: It refuses to attempt the task

exercises.feedback: Obvious breakage would be a gift, because you would catch it. What you get instead is confident, well-formed text that a native speaker would find slightly off or occasionally wrong in a way that matters.

exercises.prompt: Match each symptom to its cause.

pairs.right: No rule given about what to leave alone
Register never specified
Usage postdates the training cutoff
Thin training material for that language

exercises.prompt: Three of these are affected by the training cutoff. Which is NOT?
Tap the part it cannot deliver.

config.text: Translate this contract into Marathi and confirm it is legally accurate.

exercises.feedback: It will confirm. That is the problem. Confirmation is text, and text is what it produces. Nothing behind that sentence checked anything against Marathi contract law.

exercises.prompt: Order a workable process for translating customer-facing material.

steps: State the reader, the register, and what to leave untranslated
Translate in batches small enough to stay consistent
Have a fluent speaker check a sample
Fix the prompt, not just the output, when the sample fails

exercises.feedback: The last step is where the leverage is. Fixing a single bad translation gets you one good sentence. Fixing the instruction that caused it gets you the next thousand.

exercises.prompt: What separates localising from translating?
exercises.feedback: Currency, dates, names, examples and how directly you can say no all shift by place. A perfectly accurate translation can still read as written for somebody else.

exercises.prompt: Which of these need changing for a different country, beyond the words?

items.text: Example names in a case study

exercises.prompt: Build a localisation prompt.

tiles: Adapt the text below for readers in Tamil Nadu
keep the structure and argument order
replace examples and names with local ones
leave product names and figures untouched

exercises.feedback: The three middle tiles are the whole job. Without them the model decides for itself what counts as adaptable, and it will cheerfully localise the one number you needed left alone.

exercises.prompt: Which produces material you could publish?

config.a: Make this marketing page suitable for an Indian audience.
config.b: Adapt this marketing page for first-time buyers in India. Use rupees, Indian names in examples, and keep the three-section structure.

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase that makes the task impossible.

config.text: Localise this for our international audience so it resonates everywhere.

exercises.feedback: Localising means choosing somewhere. A version for everywhere is the version you already have.

exercises.prompt: Match each goal to what to say in the prompt.

pairs.right: Leave product names untranslated
Use formal address throughout
Replace names and places with local ones
Keep the section order unchanged

exercises.prompt: Add the guard against invented equivalents.

config.template: Translate the legal terms below into Bengali. ___
bank: If no standard equivalent exists, keep the English and say so.
config.correct: If no standard equivalent exists, keep the English and say so.

exercises.feedback: Same move as Unit 3 permitted exit. Without a way to flag a gap, the model closes it with something plausible, and a plausible-looking legal term is worse than an English one left in place.

exercises.prompt: Your translations are accurate but inconsistent across a large batch. What is the likely fix?

options.text: Pin the register in the prompt
Ask for a higher accuracy level

exercises.prompt: What lets a model resolve which noun a pronoun refers to?

options.text: Relating words by role and meaning
Following grammar rules it was given

exercises.prompt: Which of these should you specify before a translation job?
Three of these raise the risk of a wrong translation. Which does NOT?

options.text: A language with little written data
A source document that runs longer

exercises.prompt: Tap the instruction that cannot be checked.

config.text: Translate our entire help centre into Hindi, Tamil and Bengali, and make sure everything is culturally appropriate.

exercises.prompt: Match each situation to the right move.

pairs.right: Supply the context that resolves it
Ask it to flag and keep the original
Pin register once, in the instruction
Have a fluent speaker check a sample

exercises.prompt: Order a first pass at translating a product page.

steps: Decide the reader and the register
List what must not be translated
Translate a short representative section
Check that section with a fluent speaker before doing the rest

exercises.prompt: Your company is launching in a new state and the entire onboarding flow needs translating. Write a prompt that will produce output consistent enough to ship across dozens of screens.

config.goal: Produce consistent, shippable translations at scale.
config.assessed: Does the prompt fix register, name the reader, state what must stay untranslated, and give a route for terms with no equivalent?

exercises.prompt: A translated support article is grammatically perfect and reads as though it was written for somebody in another country. Write a prompt that would have localised it properly.

config.assessed: Does the rewrite distinguish what to preserve from what to adapt, rather than asking generally for a natural or appropriate result?

title: Use AI as a sparring partner

exercises.prompt: You say "I think we should raise prices by 20 percent, do you agree?" Why does it tend to agree?

options.text: It was designed to be supportive
It has no view on pricing

exercises.feedback: Look at the sentence you handed it. After a confident proposal ending in do you agree, the likeliest continuation in almost any text is some form of yes. You did not ask for an assessment. You asked for the end of that sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which prompt gets you a real critique?

config.a: I think we should raise prices by 20 percent. What do you think?
config.b: Argue against raising prices by 20 percent. Give the three strongest objections a sceptical friend would raise.

exercises.feedback: B removes agreement from the space of valid answers. You are no longer asking whether it agrees, you are asking it to do a specific job that has a shape.

exercises.prompt: Which of these invite a genuine challenge?

items.text: What would have to be true for this to fail?
Give the strongest case against this
Does this sound like a good plan?

exercises.feedback: The agreement-inviting three all leave yes available and pleasant. The others make yes an invalid response, which is the entire trick.

exercises.prompt: Tap the words that will not do what you hope.

config.text: Here is my business plan. Please review it honestly and tell me what you really think.
config.span: honestly and tell me what you really think

exercises.feedback: There is no dishonest mode being switched off. Asking for honesty adds a word, not a behaviour. What changes the output is asking for a specific adversarial job: find the assumption that breaks it, name who loses if this works.

exercises.prompt: Match what you want to how to ask for it.

pairs.right: What must be true for this to work?
How would this fail in year two?
Argue the opposite position
What would a critic say is missing?

exercises.prompt: Three of these make critique more likely. Which does NOT?
Complete the prompt so agreement is off the table.

bank: List the three strongest objections to it.
Tell me if it is good.
config.correct: List the three strongest objections to it.

exercises.prompt: What makes an adversarial prompt work?

options.text: The model tries harder when pushed

exercises.prompt: What is a system prompt for?

options.text: The first question you happen to ask

exercises.feedback: It is where standing rules live: who the assistant is, what it must always do, what it must never do. The user prompt is this request. The system prompt is every request.

exercises.prompt: Where does each instruction belong?

items.text: You are reviewing plans for someone sceptical

exercises.prompt: Why does a role help more when it is specific?

options.text: It points at a kind of writing

exercises.feedback: Saying you are a lawyer does not open a legal database. It shifts which continuations look likely, towards the kind of text lawyers write. Useful, and a much smaller claim than it sounds.

exercises.prompt: Which role produces a more useful critique?

config.a: You are an expert business consultant.
config.b: You are the person who turned this idea down last year. You were right to.

exercises.feedback: A points at a wide, bland region of business writing. B points at a specific stance with a specific reason to be unimpressed, and that stance is what you actually wanted.

exercises.prompt: Build a standing instruction for a thinking partner.

tiles: You are a sceptical reviewer of early-stage plans
always name the weakest assumption first
if a claim has no evidence, say so plainly

exercises.feedback: The third tile does more work than it looks. Without it, most of the response is warm-up before the useful part, every time.

exercises.prompt: Tap the part that changes nothing.

config.text: You are a brilliant, world-renowned strategist known for your sharp insights and deep expertise across every industry.

exercises.feedback: Praise in a role description points nowhere. There is no brilliance setting. What steers output is the specific stance and situation, not the adjectives attached to it.

exercises.prompt: Match each weak role to a sharper version.

pairs.right: You are the customer who nearly did not buy
You are the sub-editor who has to cut 30 percent
You are the auditor who has to sign this off
You are the person who will deliver this

exercises.prompt: Three of these belong in a system prompt. Which does NOT?

options.text: The tone to use every time

exercises.feedback: Figures change. Anything that changes belongs with the request, not in the standing instructions, or you will be editing your system prompt every Monday.

exercises.prompt: Why does asking for the steps before the answer often improve it?

options.text: Each step conditions the next one
It slows the model down usefully
It switches on a reasoning mode

exercises.feedback: Back to Unit 1. The answer is generated from what has already been written, so writing the intermediate steps puts them into the input that produces the conclusion. Nothing was switched on. The path was just laid down first.

exercises.prompt: You want to check whether a plan holds together. Which prompt?

config.b: List the assumptions this plan depends on. Then say which one is most likely to be wrong, and why.

exercises.prompt: Order a prompt that stress-tests a decision.

steps: State the decision and what it assumes
Ask which assumption is weakest
Ask what evidence would settle it
Ask what you would do if it turned out false

exercises.feedback: The last step is where this stops being an interesting conversation and becomes useful. An objection with no consequence attached changes nothing about what you do on Monday.

exercises.prompt: Which of these benefit from asking for steps first?

items.text: Working out whether a budget adds up
Finding the flaw in an argument

exercises.prompt: Tap what the steps cannot fix.

config.text: Think step by step and tell me exactly how much we will earn next month.
config.span: exactly how much revenue we will make

exercises.feedback: Reasoning out loud helps with problems where the answer follows from the input. It does nothing about information that is not there. You will get a confident, well-structured forecast built on numbers it invented along the way.

exercises.prompt: You run the same critique prompt twice and get different objections. What does that tell you?

options.text: One of the two runs was wrong

exercises.feedback: Worth using deliberately. Running an adversarial prompt three times surfaces a wider set of objections than any single run will, and that variety is the point rather than a defect.

exercises.prompt: Add the constraint that keeps the critique honest.

bank: Base every objection on something stated in it.
Find as many problems as you can.
config.correct: Base every objection on something stated in it.

exercises.feedback: Without it you get generic objections that would apply to any proposal. Tying each one to a line in the document is what makes the critique about your plan rather than about plans.

exercises.prompt: Match each weakness in a critique to its fix.

pairs.right: Require each to cite a line
Ask for the case against, not an opinion
Run it more than once
Ask what you should do if it is right

exercises.prompt: What is the most reliable way to stop an AI agreeing with you?

options.text: Ask it to argue one side

exercises.prompt: Standing rule, or this request?

items.text: Always cite a line for each claim
You are the auditor signing this off

exercises.prompt: Three of these sharpen a role. Which does NOT?

options.text: Giving the role a reason to doubt
Naming the situation they are in

exercises.prompt: Tap the phrase that leaves agreement wide open.

config.text: You are a genius strategist. Think step by step and honestly tell me whether my idea is any good.
config.span: whether my idea is any good

exercises.feedback: Three techniques stacked and the actual question still permits yes. The role, the steps and the appeal to honesty are all doing less than the one clause that decides what a valid answer looks like.

exercises.prompt: Order a session that pressure-tests your own plan.

steps: Set a standing role with a reason to be sceptical
Ask for the assumptions your plan rests on
Ask which is weakest and what evidence would settle it
Ask what changes if that assumption fails

exercises.prompt: Match each unit to the move it gave you.

pairs.right: Constrain what a valid answer looks like
Give it less, chosen well
Ground claims in supplied text
Decide what to preserve and what to adapt

exercises.prompt: You are about to send a proposal to someone who has to approve it, and you want it torn apart first, by something that will not be polite about it. Write the prompt.

config.goal: Get a genuine adversarial review of your own work.
config.assessed: Does the prompt assign a specific sceptical stance, remove agreement as a valid answer, tie objections to the text, and ask for something actionable?

exercises.prompt: Write a system prompt for an assistant you would use every week to think through decisions. It should behave consistently without being told again each time.

config.assessed: Does it separate standing rules from per-request detail, define prohibited as well as required behaviour, and avoid praise words that carry no instruction?
